nodes.name: Nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation
nodes.statement_short: Nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation $u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0$ with initial datum $u_0$.
nodes.label: e1.1

nodes.name: Hypothesis (i): strong monotonicity of beta
nodes.statement_short: $\beta(0)=0$, $\beta\in C^1$ and $\beta$ is strongly monotone with constant $\gamma_0>0$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii): regularity of the drift b
nodes.statement: \item[(ii)] $b\in C_b(\mathbb R^{d+1}; {{\mathbb{R}}^d})$, $b(x, \cdot) \in C^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d}; {{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ $ \forall x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ {\it such that}  $$\mbox{$\sup\{|b^i_r(x,r)|;x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d},i=1,2,$ $|r|\le M\}\le C_M,$ $\forall M>0.$}$$
nodes.statement_short: $b$ is bounded continuous, $C^1$ in $r$, with $b_r$ locally bounded in $r$ uniformly in $x$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii'): x-regularity of the drift b
nodes.statement:
\item[(ii')] $b(x,0)=0$ $\forall x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d}$, $b \in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1}; {{\mathbb{R}}^d}) $ {\it and for
		$$\delta(r):=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;\ x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\},$$we have} $\delta\in   C_b({\mathbb{R}}).$
nodes.statement_short: $b(x,0)=0$, $b\in C^1$, and $\delta(r)=\sup_x|b_x(x,r)|$ is bounded continuous.

nodes.name: Notation for components and derivatives of b
nodes.statement: Here$$b(x,u)=\{b^i(x,u)\}^d_{i=1}\mbox{ and }b^i_r=\frac{{\partial} b^i}{{\partial} r}, b_x=\big\{ \nabla_x \, b^i(x, \cdot) \big\}_{i=1}^d.$$

nodes.name: Distributional solution of the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation
nodes.statement:
By a distributional solution (in the sense of Schwartz) with initial condition $u_0\in L^1$ we mean a function $u:[0,\9)\to L^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ such that
$(u(t,\cdot)dx)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is narrowly continuous, that is,
\begin{eqnarray}
&&\lim_{t\to s}\int_{{{\mathbb{R}}^d}}u(t,x)\psi(x)dx=\int_{{{\mathbb{R}}^d}}u(s,x)\psi(x)dx,\ \forall\psi\in C_b({{\mathbb{R}}^d}),\ s\ge0,\qquad \\[2mm]
&&\displaystyle\int^\9_0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}(u(t,x){\varphi}_t(t,x)+{\beta}(u(t,x)){\Delta}{\varphi}(t,x) \\
&&\qquad+b(x,u(t,x))u(t,x))\cdot\nabla_x{\varphi}(t,x))dt\,dx=0,\nonumber\\
&&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall{\varphi}\in C^\9_0((0,\9)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d).\nonumber
\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: A narrowly continuous $L^1$-valued $u$ satisfying the weak (test-function) form of the Fokker-Planck equation.

nodes.name: Narrow continuity and weak formulation of the Fokker--Planck equation
nodes.statement:
&&\lim_{t\to s}\int_{{{\mathbb{R}}^d}}u(t,x)\psi(x)dx=\int_{{{\mathbb{R}}^d}}u(s,x)\psi(x)dx,\ \forall\psi\in C_b({{\mathbb{R}}^d}),\ s\ge0,\qquad \\[2mm]
&&\displaystyle\int^\9_0\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}(u(t,x){\varphi}_t(t,x)+{\beta}(u(t,x)){\Delta}{\varphi}(t,x) \\
&&\qquad+b(x,u(t,x))u(t,x))\cdot\nabla_x{\varphi}(t,x))dt\,dx=0,\nonumber\\
&&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall{\varphi}\in C^\9_0((0,\9)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d).\nonumber
nodes.label: e1.3

nodes.name: Notation b^*(x,u)
nodes.statement: (In the following, we shall use the notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u.$)

nodes.name: Existence of mild solutions (Barbu--Röckner)
nodes.statement: In \cite{1} it was proved, in particular, that, if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in{\mathbb{R}},$ we have $\Phi\in C^2({\mathbb{R}})$, then there is a  mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1({\mathbb{R}}^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1({\mathbb{R}}^d)$.
conclusions: there is a  mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1({\mathbb{R}}^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1({\mathbb{R}}^d)$

nodes.name: Mild solution
nodes.statement_short: The mild solution is the $L^1$ limit of the implicit-Euler time discretization $u_h$ of the Fokker-Planck equation.

nodes.name: Implicit Euler scheme for the mild solution
nodes.label: e1.6

nodes.name: Nonexpansive semigroup of mild solutions
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$.
conclusions: $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$

nodes.name: Mild solutions are distributional solutions
nodes.statement: As easily seen, any mild solution is a distributional solution but the uniqueness  follows in the class of mild solutions only.
conclusions: any mild solution is a distributional solution

nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE (introduction)
nodes.statement: dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt+\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{{\beta}(u(t,X(t))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t).
nodes.statement_short: McKean-Vlasov SDE with drift $b(X,u)$ and diffusion $(\beta(u)/u)^{1/2}/\sqrt2$ depending on the density $u$ of $X(t)$.
nodes.label: e1.7

nodes.name: Lebesgue spaces L^p and norm |.|_p
nodes.statement: Denote by $L^p({\mathbb{R}}^d)=L^p$ the  space of $p$-summable functions on $L^p$, with the norm denoted $|\cdot|_p$.

nodes.name: Sobolev spaces H^k, H^{-k} and space C_b
nodes.statement: By $H^k({{\mathbb{R}}^d})=H^k$, $k=1,2$, and $H^{-k}({{\mathbb{R}}^d})=H^{-k},$ we denote the standard Sobolev spaces on ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ and by $C_b({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ the space of continuous and bounded functions on ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$.

nodes.name: Spaces C^k and C^1_b
nodes.statement: By $C^k({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ we denote the space of continuously differentiable functions on ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ of order $k$, by $C^1_b({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ the space $\left\{u\in C^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d});\frac{{\partial} u}{{\partial} y}\in C_b({{\mathbb{R}}^d}),\ j=1,...,d\right\}.$

nodes.name: L^2 scalar product and H^1--H^{-1} pairing
nodes.statement: The scalar product in $L^2$ is denoted $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2$ and by ${}_{H^{-1}}\!\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{H^1}$ the pairing between $H^1$ and $H^{-1}.$ Of course, on $L^2\times L^2$ this coincides with $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2.$

nodes.name: H^{-1} scalar product and norm
nodes.statement:
The~scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ on $H\1$ is  taken~as
\begin{equation} \<u,v\>_{-1}=\<(I-{\Delta})\1u,v\>_2,\ \forall u,v\in H\1
\end{equation}with the corresponding norm
\begin{equation} |u|_{-1}=(\<u,u\>_{-1})^{\frac12},\ u\in H\1.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $H^{-1}$ inner product $\langle (I-\Delta)^{-1}u,v\rangle_2$ and its norm $|u|_{-1}$.

nodes.name: Spaces of Schwartz distributions D'
nodes.statement: By ${\mathcal{D}}'((0,\9)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ and ${\mathcal{D}}'({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ we denote the space of Schwartz distributions on $(0,\9)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ and ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Vector-valued Sobolev space W^{1,2}([0,T];X)
nodes.statement:
If ${\mathcal{X}}$ is a Banach space, we denote by $W^{1,2}([0,T];{\mathcal{X}})$ the infinite dimensional Sobolev space 
$\{y\in L^2(0,T;{\mathcal{X}});$ $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;{\mathcal{X}})\}$, where $\frac d{dt}$ is taken in the sense of vectorial distributions.

nodes.name: Partial derivative notation z_r, z_x
nodes.statement:
We also set, for each $z\in C^1({{\mathbb{R}}^d}\times{\mathbb{R}})$,
$$z_r(x,r)=\frac{\partial}{{\partial} r}\ z(x,r),\ \ z_x=\nabla_x z(x,r).$$

nodes.name: Norm |.| on R^d and R
nodes.statement: We shall denote the norms on ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ and ${\mathbb{R}}$  by the same symbol $|\cdot|$.

nodes.name: Brezis--Crandall uniqueness for u_t - Delta beta(u) = 0
nodes.statement: In the special case $b\equiv0$, such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1}  was established earlier in \cite{3} for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions ${\beta}$.
assumptions: for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions ${\beta}$
conclusions: such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1}  was established

nodes.name: Uniqueness of bounded distributional solutions of the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation
assumptions: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold.
conclusions: the Fokker--Planck\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)-(ii), for $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty$ the nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation has at most one bounded $L^1$ distributional solution.
nodes.label: t1

nodes.name: Solution class L^1 cap L^infty
nodes.statement: u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d}).
nodes.label: add-e5

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement:
Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d})$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
u_t-{\Delta}({\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }{\mathcal{D}}'((0,\9)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d})\vspace*{2mm}\\ 
u(0,x)=0.\end{array}
\end{equation}
(Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \forall x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d},\ r\in{\mathbb{R}}.$)

It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$ 

Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by
$$\Gamma u=(1-{\Delta})^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1({{\mathbb{R}}^d})$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$
 Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1},  we have
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
\displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma{\Delta}({\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\
y(0)=0,\end{array}
\end{equation}
where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$  (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.)

Assume first that, in addition,
\begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}).
\end{equation}


Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2}  with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that
$$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that
$$\begin{array}{l}
\displaystyle\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<{\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2
=\<\Gamma({\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vspace*{2mm}\\ 
\qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\end{array}$$ 
By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{r}
\displaystyle\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+{\gamma}_0|u(t)|^2_2
\le\<{\beta}(u_1(t))-{\beta}(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vspace*{2mm}\\
\qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\end{array}
\end{equation}
We note that
\begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \forall f\in L^2.
\end{equation}
We also have
\begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \forall F\in (L^2)^d.
\end{equation}This  yields
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll}
|\<{\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|{\beta}(u_1)-{\beta}(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} 
\le{\beta}_M|u|_2|u|_{-1}
\end{array}\end{equation}and
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
\left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vspace*{2mm}\\
\qquad\le
2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vspace*{2mm}\\
\qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1},
\end{array}
\end{equation}
where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and
$$\begin{array}{lcl}
{\beta}_M&=&\displaystyle\sup\{{\beta}'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vspace*{2mm}\\ 
b_M&=&\displaystyle\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d},\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vspace*{2mm}\\&\le&
\sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\} < \infty \end{array}$$
by (ii).

By \eqref{e2.3}--\eqref{e2.7}, we get
$$\begin{array}{r}
\displaystyle\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+{\gamma}_0|u(t)|^2_{2}
\le({\beta}_M+2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)
|u(t)|^{}_2|u(t)|^{}_{-1},\\\hfill\mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\end{array}$$
This yields
$$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\forall t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed.
To conclude the proof, we shall prove

\begin{claim} If $u$ is a distributional solution to \eqref{e1.1} satisfying \eqref{add-e5}, then \eqref{add-e6} holds.
\end{claim}

\noindent{\bf Proof of Claim \ref{add-l1}.} $1^\circ$. We shall first assume   that $u$ satisfies   the stronger initial condition
\begin{equation} \mbox{essential }\lim_{t\to0} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |u(t,x)-u_0(x)|dx=0.
\end{equation}
Next, we consider the truncated function
\begin{equation} \beta_M(r)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\beta(r)&\mbox{ if }|r|\le M,\vspace*{2mm}\\
\beta(M)+\beta'(M)(r-M)&\mbox{ if }r>M,\vspace*{2mm}\\
\beta(-M)+\beta'(-M)(r+M)&\mbox{ if }r<-M,\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}where $M=\|u\|_{L^\9(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d)}.$

We set
$$f(t,x)\equiv b^*(x,u(t,x)),\ \ f_\nu=f*\rho_\nu,\ \ \nu>0,$$where $\rho_\nu$ is a standard mollifier on ${\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}$ and $b^*(x,u)\equiv b(x,u)u$.

We note that in equation \eqref{e1.1} one can take $\beta\equiv\beta_M$ because $|u|_\9\le M.$

We consider the equations
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
\widetilde u_t-\Delta\beta_M(\widetilde u)+{\rm div}(f)=0\mbox{ in }(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d,\vspace*{2mm}\\
\widetilde u(0)=u_0,\end{array}\qquad
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
(\widetilde u_\nu)_t-\Delta\beta_M(\widetilde u_\nu)+{\rm div}(f_\nu)=0\mbox{ in }(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d,\vspace*{2mm}\\
\widetilde u_\nu(0)=u_0.\end{array}
\end{equation}
Clearly, \eqref{add-e9} has a unique solution $\widetilde u$ satisfying \eqref{add-e6}, i.e.,
\begin{equation} \widetilde u \in L^2(0,T;H^1),\ \widetilde u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}),
\end{equation}
while $\widetilde u_\nu$ is more regular, that is,   additionally to \eqref{add-e11} it satisfies
\begin{equation} \widetilde u_\nu\in L^\9((0,T)\times {\mathbb{R}}^d)\cap C^1([0,T];L^1),
\end{equation}because the operator $u\to-\Delta\beta_M(u)$ is $m$-accretive in $L^1({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ and $u_0\in(L^1\cap L^\9)({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, ${\rm div}\,f_\nu\in(L^1\cap L^\9)((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d)$. 
It is also clear that
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle\lim_{\nu\to0} \widetilde u_\nu=\widetilde u
&\mbox{ strongly in }L^2(0,T;H\1).\end{array}
\end{equation}
To prove the claim, we are going to show that
\begin{equation} \widetilde u=u,\mbox{ a.e. in }(0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d.
\end{equation}
To this end, we shall invoke an argument due to Brezis \& Crandall \cite{3}.

 Namely, we subtract equations \eqref{e1.1}, \eqref{add-e10} and get
 $$(\widetilde u_\nu- u)_t-\Delta(\beta(\widetilde u_\nu)-\beta(u)=-{\rm div}(f_\nu-f)\mbox{ in }{\mathcal{D}}'((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d),$$
 $$\mbox{essential }\lim_{t\to0}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}|\widetilde u_\nu(t,x)-u(t,x)|dx=0.$$
 We set $z_\nu=\widetilde u_\nu-u$, $h_\nu=\beta(\widetilde u_\nu)-\beta(u)$ and get
 \begin{equation} (z_\nu)_t-\Delta h_\nu=-{\rm div}(f_\nu-f)\mbox{   in }{\mathcal{D}}'((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^d),
 \end{equation}
\begin{equation} \mbox{essential }\lim_{t\to0}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}|z_\nu(t,x)|dx=0.
\end{equation}
Arguing as in \cite{3} (proof of Proposition 1), we set
$$g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t)=(B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu),z_\nu),\ B_{\varepsilon}=({\varepsilon} I-\Delta)^{-1},$$where $(\ ,\ )$ denotes the inner product in $L^2=L^2({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, and get
$$(g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t))_t=2({\varepsilon} B_{\varepsilon}(h_\nu)-h_\nu,z_\nu(t))+2(f_\nu-f,\nabla B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu))$$and, therefore (we note that $(h_\nu,z_\nu)\ge0$),
 \begin{equation} g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t)\le2\displaystyle\int^t_0{\varepsilon}(B_{\varepsilon}(h_\nu(s)),z_\nu(s))ds
+2\displaystyle\int^t_0((f_\nu-f)(s),\nabla B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s)))ds,
\end{equation}because, by \eqref{add-e14'}, we have, since $z_\nu\in L^\9\cap L^1$,
 \begin{equation} g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(0^+)=\mbox{essential }\lim_{t\to0}(B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(t),z_\nu(t))=0.
\end{equation}
Recalling that, for a.e. $s\in[0,T]$,
$${\varepsilon} B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s))-\Delta B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s))=z_\nu(s),$$we get
$$g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(s)=(B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s)),z_\nu(s))={\varepsilon}|B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s))|^2_{L^2}+|\nabla B_{\varepsilon}(z_\nu(s))|^2_{L^2}$$
and so, by \eqref{add-e15}, we have
 \begin{equation} g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t)\le2\displaystyle\int^t_0{\varepsilon}(B_{\varepsilon} h_\nu(s),z_\nu(s))ds
+\displaystyle\int^t_0|(f_\nu-f)(s)|^2_{L^2}ds+\displaystyle\int^t_0 g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(s)ds.
\end{equation}Hence, by Gronwall's inequality,
 \begin{equation} g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t)\le\int^t_0(2{\varepsilon}(B_{\varepsilon} (h_\nu(s)),z_\nu(s))+|(f_\nu-f)(s)|^2_{L^2})e^{t-s}ds.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by Lemma 1 in \cite{3} we have for a.e. $s\in[0,T]$ and also in $L^1(0,T)$
 \begin{equation} \lim_{{\varepsilon}\to0}({\varepsilon} B_{\varepsilon} (h_\nu(s)),z_\nu(s))=0.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{add-e18}, this yields
 \begin{equation} (G*z_\nu(t),z_\nu(t))\le\int^t_0|(f_\nu-f)(s)|^2_{L^2}e^{t-s}ds,\end{equation}
since $$\lim_{{\varepsilon}\to0}g^\nu_{\varepsilon}(t)=((-\Delta)^{-1}z_\nu(t),z_\nu(t))=(G*z_\nu(t),z_\nu(t)),$$where $G$ is the classical Newtonian Green function. We note that the  latter  inner product is well defined, since $z_\nu\in\displaystyle\bigcap_{p\in[1,\9]}L^p$ and hence $G*z_\nu\in L^{\frac{2d}{d-2}}.$ Letting $\nu\to0$ in \eqref{add-e22a}, we find
$$\lim_{\nu\to0}(G*z_\nu(t),z_\nu(t))=0.$$
In particular, $\xymatrix{z_\nu(t)\ar[r]_{\ \ \nu\to0}&0}$ in $H^{-1}$. nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE
nodes.statement:
Consider for $T\in(0,\9)$ and $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$ the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation (SDE)
\begin{equation} \begin{array}{l}
dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt
+\displaystyle\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{{\beta}(u(t,X(t)))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t),\vspace*{2mm}\\
\hfill 0\le t\le T,\\
u(0,\cdot)=\xi_0,\end{array}\end{equation}on ${{\mathbb{R}}^d}$. 
Here, $W(t),\ t\ge0,$ is an $({\mathcal{F}}_t)$-Brownian motion on a probability space $(\Omega,{\mathcal{F}},\mathbb{P})$ with normal filtration ${\mathcal{F}}_t$, $t\ge0,$ $\xi_0:\Omega\to{{\mathbb{R}}^d}$ is ${\mathcal{F}}_0$-measurable such that $$\mathbb{P}\circ\xi^{-1}_0(dx)=u_0(x)dx,$$ and $u(t,x)=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}}{dx}\,(x)$ is the Lebesgue density of the marginal law $\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}=\mathbb{P}\circ X(t)\1$ of the solution process $X(t)$, $t\ge0$.

nodes.statement_short: SDE whose drift and diffusion depend on the Lebesgue density $u(t,\cdot)$ of the law of $X(t)$, with initial law $u_0dx$.

$$u(t,\cdot):=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}}{dx},\ \ \widetilde u(t,\cdot):=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{\widetilde X(t)}}{dx},$$we have

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.section: 4 Uniqueness in law of the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs)
nodes.statement_short: Itô's formula reduces to the Fokker-Planck equation, so the marginals coincide by Theorem 2.1; then linearized uniqueness (Theorem 3.1) and Trevisan's superposition lemma give equality of laws.

nodes.name: Marginals coincide
nodes.statement: By It\^o's formula, both $u$ and $\widetilde u$ satisfy the (nonlinear) Fokker--Planck\ equation \eqref{e1.1} in the sense of Schwartz distributions. Hence, by Theorem \ref{t1}, $u=\widetilde u$.
nodes.section: 4 Uniqueness in law of the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs)
nodes.statement_short: By Itô's formula the marginal densities solve the Fokker-Planck equation, so they agree by Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Martingale problem for the linear Kolmogorov operator
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, again by It\^o's formula, $\mathbb{P}\circ X\1$ and $\mathbb{P}\circ\widetilde X\1$ satisfy the martingale problem with the initial condition $u_0dx$ for the linear Komogorov operator
$$L_u:=\Phi(u){\Delta}+b(\cdot,u)\cdot\nabla,$$where $\Phi(u)=\frac{{\beta}(u)}u,$ $u\in{\mathbb{R}}.$
nodes.section: 4 Uniqueness in law of the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs)
nodes.statement_short: Both laws solve the martingale problem for the linear operator $L_u$.

Hence, by Theorem \ref{t5}, the assertion follows by Lemma 2.12 in \cite{4}. 

Here, for $s\in[0,T]$, the set $\mathcal{R}_{[s,T]}$, which appears in that lemma, is chosen to be the set of all narrowly continuous, probability measure-valued solutions of \eqref{e3.1} having for each $t\in[s,T]$ a density \mbox{$v(t,\cdot)\in L^\9$} with respect to  Lebesgue measure such that \mbox{$v\in L^\9((0,T)\times{{\mathbb{R}}^d}).$}
nodes.section: 4 Uniqueness in law of the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs)
nodes.statement_short: Linearized uniqueness plus Lemma 2.12 of Trevisan gives uniqueness of the martingale problem, hence equal laws.
